reference.source: Auerbach's Wilderness Medicine / Bove and Davis' Diving Medicine
clinicalPearls: An inflammatory cold injury, not a freezing injury, caused by repeated exposure to cold but non-freezing, often damp conditions
Presents with itchy or painful erythematous to violaceous papules, plaques, or nodules on acral sites such as toes, fingers, ears, and nose
Lesions typically appear hours after cold exposure and may blister or ulcerate in severe cases
Distinguished from frostbite by the absence of tissue freezing and from Raynaud phenomenon by the fixed inflammatory lesions rather than transient colour change
Rewarming should be gradual, with keeping the affected part dry and warm and avoiding further cold exposure
Persistent, recurrent, or atypical pernio may be associated with connective tissue disease (notably lupus) and warrants further evaluation
Prevention through warm, dry, layered clothing and avoiding damp cold is the mainstay of management
reference.pathophysiology: Chilblains represent an abnormal inflammatory response to cold, non-freezing exposure. Cold-induced vasoconstriction of dermal vessels, followed by a poorly regulated inflammatory and vascular reaction on rewarming, produces localised tissue oedema, a perivascular inflammatory infiltrate, and the characteristic tender discoloured acral lesions. Unlike frostbite there is no ice crystal formation, so the injury is inflammatory rather than a direct freezing necrosis. A subset of cases reflects an underlying autoimmune or connective tissue disorder that predisposes to the exaggerated vascular response.
additionalDifferentials: Lupus pernio and other connective tissue disease-related vasculopathy
Trench foot / immersion foot (non-freezing cold injury of prolonged wet exposure)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis based on history of cold, damp exposure and characteristic acral lesions
Autoimmune screen (including antinuclear antibodies) in recurrent, severe, or atypical cases
Cold agglutinins and cryoglobulins where an alternative vasculopathy is suspected
Skin biopsy in diagnostic uncertainty or when connective tissue disease is considered
Assessment for peripheral vascular disease in older patients
redFlags: Ulceration, necrosis, or secondary infection of lesions
Features suggesting underlying connective tissue disease or systemic vasculitis
Persistent lesions unresponsive to cold avoidance
Signs of concurrent freezing injury (frostbite) after severe exposure
reference.prognosis: Acute chilblains usually resolve over one to three weeks with cold avoidance and supportive care; chronic or recurrent perniosis can persist through cold seasons and, when linked to autoimmune disease, follows the course of the underlying condition.
pitfalls: Mistaking pernio for frostbite and applying inappropriately aggressive rewarming
Failing to investigate recurrent or atypical cases for connective tissue disease
Rubbing or applying direct heat, which can aggravate the inflammatory injury
Overlooking secondary infection of blistered or ulcerated lesions
management: Cold avoidance with gradual rewarming, keeping the affected parts dry and warm using insulation, gloves and warm footwear, is the mainstay
Smoking cessation to reduce peripheral vasoconstriction
Topical corticosteroids for symptomatic lesions, with wound care for blistering or ulceration
Vasodilator therapy with a calcium-channel blocker such as nifedipine for severe or recurrent perniosis
Investigate for and manage underlying connective tissue disease, notably lupus, in persistent, recurrent or atypical cases
Referral to dermatology or rheumatology for refractory or autoimmune-associated disease
